title: 11 AI tools every product manager should learn
desc: The AI tools PMs use for research, writing, prototyping and automation, what each is best for, and the order to learn them in.
body:
AI tools now cover most of a PM's week: research, writing, design, prototyping and the repetitive work in between. You don't need all of them. You need to know which tool fits which job, and to be fluent in a few. Here's how the AI Tools Lab groups them.

Thinking and writing: Claude

Use Claude for interview synthesis, PRD drafts and critique, competitor research and data analysis. Projects keep your product context in one place, and connectors bring in Gmail, Calendar, Drive and Slack. Start here: it pays off the fastest.

Building: Claude Code, Lovable and Replit

  • Claude Code reads and edits real projects, pushes to GitHub and deploys prototypes. Best when you want full control.
  • Lovable goes from a prompt to a web app with a database, login and payments. Best for fast MVPs.
  • Replit builds and hosts full-stack apps in the browser. Good for quick internal tools.

Design: Figma and Figma Make

Design screens, build click-through prototypes and run workshops in FigJam. Figma Make generates working prototypes from a design, and Figma's MCP server lets Claude Code build from your designs.

Docs: Notion and PRD tools

Keep a product hub in Notion, write and critique PRDs with AI, and turn specs into tickets automatically.

Automation: Zapier, Make and n8n

Connect Gmail, Slack, Sheets and forms so routine work runs by itself. Zapier is the easiest to start with, Make is better for visual multi-step flows, and n8n is the most flexible and can run on your own server.

Customer-facing AI: chatbots and voice agents

WhatsApp and website chatbots answer customers with a safe handoff to people. Voice agents built on platforms like Vapi or Retell answer calls and book appointments for clinics, salons and shops.

Learn concepts, not buttons: triggers, tools, memory, evaluation and permissions last longer than any interface.

The order we recommend

Claude first, then Figma, then one builder (Lovable or Claude Code), then one automation tool. Add chatbots and voice agents when you're ready for a capstone. Every class is free in the AI Tools Lab.

title: How to become a product manager in 2026: a practical roadmap
desc: A step-by-step plan to move into product management from any background, with the skills, projects and applications that matter.
body:
Product management has no single entry path. People move into PM roles from engineering, design, sales, operations, consulting and straight out of college. What they have in common is proof that they can find a real problem, decide what to build and work with a team to ship it. This roadmap is about building that proof.

1. Understand what a PM actually does

A product manager is responsible for outcomes, not output. You decide which problems are worth solving, align engineers, designers and business teams around a plan, and measure whether the change worked. Start with Module 1 of the handbook, which covers the PM decision loop and how the role differs from project management, design and engineering.

2. Learn the core skills in order

  • Discovery: interviews, surveys and jobs-to-be-done to find problems worth solving.
  • Prioritisation: frameworks like RICE, Kano and MoSCoW, and the judgement to use them well.
  • Communication: clear PRDs, stakeholder updates and saying no with reasons.
  • Metrics: choosing a north-star metric, reading funnels and running A/B tests.
  • Tech and AI basics: enough to ask engineers the right questions and to prototype with AI tools.

3. Build three portfolio case studies

Hiring managers want to see how you think. Pick products you use and write case studies that show the whole loop: the problem, evidence, options you considered, what you chose and how you would measure success. One UX redesign, one growth or metrics case and one product strategy case is a strong mix. Our case studies show the format.

A case study with real user evidence beats ten slides of opinions.

4. Use AI tools to show you can build

In 2026, PMs who can prototype stand out. A clickable Figma flow, a Lovable app or a small automation in n8n turns your idea into something an interviewer can try. The 12-week plan walks you through one tool a week.

5. Apply with a focused story

  • Target roles where your background is an advantage, such as a fintech PM role if you've worked in banking.
  • Rewrite your resume around outcomes: what changed because of your work, with numbers.
  • Practise product sense, metrics and behavioural rounds out loud before real interviews.

Where to start this week

Read Module 1, pick the product you'll write your first case study about, and set aside five hours a week. If you'd like a plan built around your background, book a mentoring call.

title: How to write a PM case study that gets you interviews
desc: A simple structure for product case studies, the evidence hiring managers look for, and mistakes to avoid.
body:
Your case study is a sample of your thinking. Recruiters skim it in a minute, and hiring managers read it to decide whether to interview you. Both want the same thing: a clear problem, real evidence and a sensible decision.

A structure that works

  • Context: the product, the user and why this problem matters to the business.
  • Problem: one sentence, specific enough to be measurable.
  • Evidence: interviews, a short survey, reviews, screenshots of the current flow, or data.
  • Options: two or three solutions you considered, and the trade-offs between them.
  • Decision: what you'd build first and why, ideally with a prototype.
  • Metrics: the primary metric, guardrail metrics and how you'd run the test.
  • Risks and next steps: what could go wrong and what you'd learn next.

What makes it stand out

Real users. Even five short interviews make your case stronger than any framework. Our Case Study Library includes a ride-hailing case (Uber and Ola-style cancellation rates) you can use as a model.

Show your reasoning, not just your answer.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Redesigning the whole app instead of one flow.
  • Listing features without saying which problem they solve.
  • Made-up metrics with no baseline or source.
  • Forty slides. Five to ten clear pages is enough.

Get feedback before you apply

Ask a PM to review it, or book a portfolio review. One round of feedback often turns a good case study into a great one.

title: How to become a PM in 2027: a practical roadmap
desc: A nine-month roadmap to becoming a product manager in 2027: the core skills, the AI skills employers now ask for, portfolio case studies, interview practice and job search, with a link to a free resource at every step.
body:
Product management is still one of the best-paid, most-asked-for routes into tech, but the way people get in has changed. In 2027, a PM is expected to understand AI well enough to decide where it helps, where it hurts, and how to measure the difference. This roadmap is a practical sequence you can follow over about nine months, with a link to the free resource for each step.

What the job market is asking for. In our research of 46 product-manager job records, 38 showed requirement text, and 19 of those asked for a stated number of years of experience. SQL appeared in 6, A/B testing in 5, and writing requirements or user stories in 4. Fewer records named AI skills yet, which tells you the bar is still rising rather than already set. Treat these counts as directional: most postings could not be opened in full during the research, so check the roles you are targeting before you rely on them.

Step 1: Understand what a PM actually does (weeks 1 to 3)

A product manager owns outcomes, not output. You decide which problems are worth solving, get engineers, designers and business teams aligned on a plan, and check whether the change worked. Many people apply for PM roles without being able to explain this loop, and interviewers notice.

Read the PM Master Handbook first. It covers the decision loop and how the PM role differs from project management, design and engineering. Download the PM Master Handbook (free PDF). Then read the programme overview to see how the skills are sequenced: AI Product Management programme.

Goal by the end of step 1: write a one-page explanation of one product you use daily, covering the user, the job it does, the metric that shows it works, and one thing you would change.

Step 2: Learn the five core skills in order (weeks 3 to 10)

  • Discovery. Interviews, surveys and jobs-to-be-done to find problems worth solving. Practise by interviewing five people about a task they do every week.
  • Prioritisation. RICE, Kano and MoSCoW, and the judgement to know when a framework is the wrong tool. Use the PM toolkit for templates.
  • Writing requirements. A clear product requirements document (PRD) and a business requirements document (BRD). Try the PRD writer, then compare your draft with the PRD library. For the difference between a BRD and a functional requirements document, see the BRD and FRD guide.
  • Metrics. Choosing a north-star metric, reading a funnel, and knowing when a result is noise. The practice tests include metric questions with worked answers.
  • Tech and AI basics. Enough to ask engineers the right questions and to prototype. Start with the AI skills map, which lists every AI skill and where to learn it.

Step 3: Add the AI skills that 2027 roles expect (weeks 8 to 16)

AI features are moving from experiments into production, so product teams need PMs who can run them. These four AI skills are the ones our courses teach to product managers:

  • Evaluation. How to write a golden test set, define what a good answer is, and set a release bar. Start with the AI evals course.
  • AI product strategy. Where AI creates value, when to build versus buy, and how to price it. See AI product strategy and AI pricing.
  • Governance and responsible AI. Privacy, bias, human approval points and incident response. See AI governance.
  • Hands-on understanding. You do not need to code to be a strong AI PM, but you should have built something. The AI Master Course has a six-week path with a free handbook and a starter project you can run yourself.

Our skills map groups all of these with the courses on the site: AI Courses.

Step 4: Build three portfolio case studies (weeks 12 to 24)

Hiring managers want to see how you think. A portfolio case study shows the whole loop: the problem, the evidence, the options you considered, what you chose and how you would measure success. Build three, each about two pages:

  1. One consumer product redesign, for example a banking or food app you use.
  2. One growth or metrics case, where you find a funnel problem and propose a test.
  3. One AI feature case, where you define what good looks like, the risks, and the evaluation plan. The AI product strategy material and the evals course give you the frameworks.

Read how to write a PM case study that gets you interviews before you start, and use the free resources page for templates.

Step 5: Prepare for interviews (weeks 20 to 30)

PM interviews typically cover four areas: product sense (design a feature), analytical thinking (diagnose a metric change), execution (prioritise and plan), and, for AI roles, AI product judgement. Practise each one out loud and time yourself.

  • Question bank: PM interview questions with answers, and the AI PM question bank (50 questions with model answers).
  • Mock rounds: the interview practice hub and speaking coach give feedback on how you explain an answer.
  • System design for PMs: system design for product managers teaches the architecture questions you will hear in AI roles.

Step 6: Find the roles and apply with a plan (months 6 to 9)

A common rule of thumb is to apply where you meet most of the stated requirements, and to tailor your CV to the wording of each posting. Keep a tracker with the company, the role, the date and the person you contacted. Look at the job board for current openings, and read the AI jobs 2027 roadmap to see which AI roles fit your background.

Referrals usually help more than cold applications. Share your case studies with people in product roles, and ask one specific question rather than for a job.

A nine-month timeline on one page

MonthsFocusOutput you can show
1Role and handbook (step 1)One-page product teardown
2 to 3Core skills (step 2)PRD and prioritisation exercise
3 to 4AI skills (step 3)An evals plan for one AI feature
4 to 6Portfolio (step 4)Three case studies
6 to 8Interviews (step 5)Timed answers scored against a rubric
7 to 9Applications and referrals (step 6)Tracker with at least 30 targeted applications

The timeline assumes 8 to 10 hours a week alongside a job. Those with more time can compress it; those with less should stretch it rather than skip the portfolio.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Collecting courses instead of building things. Each step should end with an output you can show.
  • Describing features instead of outcomes. Every case study needs a metric and a result, even a small one.
  • Ignoring AI because it feels technical. In 2027, an AI product decision is a PM decision.
  • Applying widely without tailoring. Ten tailored applications beat fifty generic ones.
